newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK ACTOR STRIKE SUSPENDED, PROTESTS REMAIN.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK ACTOR STRIKE SUSPENDED, PROTESTS REMAIN.

text.p: Slovak actors said on Tuesday suspended their month-long strike but warned they would remain on strike alert until problems in the cultural sector were resolved.

"All the striking theatres will resume performances on Wednesday, but the actors are ready to return to a 'hot strike' immediately if the situation again deteriorates," an official of the Theatre Trade Union told Reuters.

She said the decision to suspend the strike was based on an appeal by President Michal Kovac to the actors to return to the stage, while urging parliament and the government to deal seriously with the crisis in culture.
However, artists, students and the opposition have said they would not stop organising protest actions, such as peacful demonstrations.

The strike and ongoing protests by Slovakia's cultural community against government interference in the arts has become a rallying point against the coalition of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar and involves students, some Roman Catholic bishops and even Kovac.

The actors' strike, which has closed most Bratislava theatres and others in the country, was sparked by last year's sacking of the general director and artistic directors of the National Theatre, and the setting of regional cultural administrations to control theatres, art galleries, libraries and other cultural activities.
Government officials have said the actors and students are being manipulated by the opposition.
The affair came to a head earlier in March when Culture Minister Ivan Hudec called in police to end a sit-in at his ministry by actors and supporters, including several opposition parliamentarians.

"The problems of culture... have become a matter of the entire society," Kovac said in a statement, obtained by Reuters on Tuesday. "I call on parliament and the government...to open a dialogue to put in order conditions in culture as soon as possible."
Earlier this month Kovac added his voice to calls for Hudec to step down. But the minister, backed by the ruling coalition survived a parliamentary no-confidence vote last week.
The unrest comes in the runnup to referendums on whether Slovaks wish to join North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and on whether the president should be elected by direct popular vote.
Meciar's government claims Slovakia wants to be among the first new members of the NATO but its chances seem to have slipped after U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of democratic reform.

Last weekend, Meciar admitted the country appeared to have dropped out from the first round of NATO enlargement, but said this was more result of a division of the global spheres of interest between the Russia and the United States, than a consequence of his controversial domestic policy.
